2. STEP 1 — INDEPENDENT DESIGN CLASSIFICATION & TOOL SELECTION (`RISK_OF_BIAS.md` §1):
   Classify the study's actual design from its Methods section, then select the matching appraisal tool:
   - `"RoB 2 (parallel-trial variant)"`: Individually randomized controlled trial. Rate all 5 domains (`D1` Randomization process; `D2` Deviations from intended interventions; `D3` Missing outcome data; `D4` Measurement of the outcome; `D5` Selection of the reported result) as `"Low"`, `"Some concerns"`, or `"High"`, and overall rating as `"Low"`, `"Some concerns"`, or `"High"`.
   - `"RoB 2 (cluster-randomized trials variant)"`: Cluster-randomized trial (villages, compounds, neighbourhoods, schools, utilities randomized as clusters). Rate all 6 domains (`D1a` Randomization process; `D1b` Timing of identification or recruitment of participants within clusters; `D2` Deviations from intended interventions; `D3` Missing outcome data; `D4` Measurement of the outcome; `D5` Selection of the reported result) as `"Low"`, `"Some concerns"`, or `"High"`, and overall rating as `"Low"`, `"Some concerns"`, or `"High"`.
   - `"ROBINS-I"`: Non-randomized study of an intervention / policy with a genuine comparator (DiD, IV, RDD, PSM, ITS, controlled before-after, comparative longitudinal/panel evaluation). Rate all 7 domains (`D1` Bias due to confounding; `D2` Bias in selection of participants into the study; `D3` Bias in classification of interventions; `D4` Bias due to deviations from intended interventions; `D5` Bias due to missing data; `D6` Bias in measurement of outcomes; `D7` Bias in selection of the reported result — note `No information` honestly if no pre-analysis plan/protocol exists) as `"Low"`, `"Moderate"`, `"Serious"`, `"Critical"`, or `"No information"`, and overall rating in the same vocabulary. Do NOT assign single-case histories with no comparator arm to ROBINS-I!
   - `"JBI Critical Appraisal Checklist for Analytical Cross Sectional Studies"`: Quantitative cross-sectional survey / observational regression without a quasi-experimental intervention structure. Rate all 8 items (`Q1` Inclusion criteria in sample clearly defined; `Q2` Study subjects and setting described in detail; `Q3` Exposure measured validly and reliably; `Q4` Objective, standard criteria used for measurement of condition; `Q5` Confounding factors identified; `Q6` Strategies to deal with confounding factors stated; `Q7` Outcomes measured validly and reliably; `Q8` Appropriate statistical analysis used) as `"Yes"`, `"No"`, `"Unclear"`, or `"Not applicable"`. Provide overall narrative judgment (`"Low concern"`, `"Some concern"`, or `"High concern"` — no numeric score).
   - `"JBI Critical Appraisal Checklist for Cohort Studies"`: Observational comparative cohort design (not framed as a ROBINS-I intervention). Rate all 11 items (`Q1` Similar groups from same population; `Q2` Exposures measured similarly; `Q3` Exposure measured validly/reliably; `Q4` Confounding factors identified; `Q5` Strategies to deal with confounding stated; `Q6` Participants free of outcome at start; `Q7` Outcomes measured validly/reliably; `Q8` Follow-up time reported and sufficient; `Q9` Follow-up complete or loss explored; `Q10` Strategies to address incomplete follow-up utilized; `Q11` Appropriate statistical analysis used) as `"Yes"`, `"No"`, `"Unclear"`, or `"Not applicable"`, plus narrative overall judgment (`"Low concern"`, `"Some concern"`, `"High concern"`).
   - `"CASP Qualitative Checklist"`: Primary qualitative study (interviews, ethnography, focus groups, qualitative documentary/field case study). Rate all 10 items (`Q1` Clear statement of aims; `Q2` Qualitative methodology appropriate; `Q3` Research design appropriate to address aims; `Q4` Recruitment strategy appropriate to aims; `Q5` Data collected in a way that addressed research issue; `Q6` Relationship between researcher and participants adequately considered [reflexivity]; `Q7` Ethical issues considered; `Q8` Data analysis sufficiently rigorous; `Q9` Clear statement of findings; `Q10` How valuable is the research [narrative assessment]). Rate Q1-Q9 `"Yes"`, `"No"`, or `"Can't tell"`, and Q10 narratively; give narrative `overall_rating` (e.g. `"Low methodological concern"`, `"Moderate concern (X Can't tell / No items)"`, `"High methodological concern"` — no numeric score).
   - `"MMAT (Mixed Methods Appraisal Tool)"`: Genuine mixed-methods primary study combining qualitative AND quantitative empirical components (do NOT assign purely quantitative or purely qualitative studies to MMAT). Rate Screening `S1`-`S2`, Qualitative `1.1`-`1.5`, the matching Quantitative 5-item block (`2.1`-`2.5` randomized, `3.1`-`3.5` non-randomized, or `4.1`-`4.5` descriptive), AND Mixed-Methods integration `5.1`-`5.5` (`5.1` adequate rationale for mixed methods; `5.2` components effectively integrated; `5.3` outputs of integration adequately interpreted; `5.4` divergences/inconsistencies adequately addressed; `5.5` components adhere to quality criteria of each tradition) as `"Yes"`, `"No"`, or `"Can't tell"`. Per MMAT 2018 rules, NEVER compute a numeric score; provide a concise criterion-grounded narrative `overall_rating` noting that overall quality cannot exceed the weakest component.
   - `"AMSTAR 2"`: Secondary systematic review, meta-analysis, or scoping review with an explicit systematic search/screening method (NEVER apply AMSTAR 2 to non-systematic narrative literature reviews!). Rate all 16 items `Q1`-`Q16` (explicitly marking critical domains `Q2`, `Q4`, `Q7`, `Q9`, `Q11`, `Q13`, `Q15`) as `"Yes"`, `"Partial Yes"` (where applicable), `"No"`, or `"Not applicable (no meta-analysis)"`, and apply AMSTAR 2 overall confidence (`"High"`, `"Moderate"`, `"Low"`, `"Critically Low"`).
   - `"Legal Institutional Evidence Appraisal Framework"`: Doctrinal-empirical hybrid, jurimetric analysis, or institutional/legal-historical case study that fits NONE of the six conventional designs above. Rate all 13 narrative domains (`D1` Legal source accuracy; `D2` Jurisdictional specificity; `D3` Exposure definition; `D4` Outcome definition; `D5` Sampling transparency; `D6` Selection process; `D7` Measurement transparency; `D8` Causal identification; `D9` Treatment of confounding; `D10` Institutional context; `D11` Replication potential; `D12` Coding transparency; `D13` Researcher reflexivity) as `"strong"`, `"adequate"`, `"weak"`, or `"not assessable"`. Explicitly frame `overall_rating` as a structured non-validated judgment (NEVER a numeric composite score!).
   - `"NONE"`: Use when the study fits NONE of the listed instruments (e.g., pure mathematical/simulation optimization model with no empirical sample, or non-systematic narrative essay/review with no primary empirical method and no systematic search). Set `overall_rating = "NOT APPLICABLE (design fits no listed tool)"`, explain clearly in `why_tool_chosen` and `overall_narrative_summary` rather than forcing an inappropriate checklist, and still fill the 7 `cross_tool_domains` honestly from the paper!

cross_tool_domains.attrition: Moderate-to-high concern (cross-sectional nonresponse rather than longitudinal panel attrition): in Ontario, 17 of 45 listed communities could not be reached/confirmed and 20 of 28 confirmed communities refused or did not return calls (PDF Page 5); in British Columbia, the total number of conference attendees approached is unreported (unknown overall survey response rate) and item nonresponse was substantial on sensitive items such as salary, job satisfaction, paid vacation, and years of experience (PDF Pages 5, 7, 10).
cross_tool_domains.confounding: High concern (uncontrolled): descriptive exploratory mixed-methods study with no comparator group, stratification, or multivariable adjustment for potential confounders such as community remoteness zone, plant treatment complexity, system size, or band revenue base; quantitative analysis is limited to univariate counts and percentages in Microsoft Excel (PDF Pages 5-6, 14).
cross_tool_domains.legal_measurement_quality: Weak-to-adequate (contextual description strong, empirical operationalization weak): the paper accurately contextualizes Bill S-8 (Safe Drinking Water for First Nations Act), the AANDC 80:20 O&M funding formula, Band Council governance authority, and Isaac v. British Columbia (Workers' Compensation Board) (1994) (PDF Pages 3, 14-15), but empirically measures regulatory certification adequacy solely via unverified operator self-report without checking provincial certification registries, plant classifications, or band council records (PDF Pages 5, 7).
cross_tool_domains.measurement_bias: High concern: Ontario interviews were recorded via interviewer handwritten notes rather than audio recordings due to operator fear of repercussions (PDF Page 5); BC data relied entirely on an unpiloted, unvalidated self-report questionnaire that permitted contradictory responses on job satisfaction (3 respondents checked both satisfied and unsatisfied; PDF Page 10), contained an internal arithmetic discrepancy in reported salary counts (50 + 16 + 33 = 99 reported responses out of N = 79; PDF Page 7), and omitted x-axis category labels in Figures 3 and 5 (PDF Pages 9, 13).
cross_tool_domains.outcome_measurement_quality: Weak (indirect perceptual/self-reported outcomes only): no objective drinking water quality tests, drinking water advisory logs, infrastructure inspection records, or administrative payroll/turnover records were collected; outcomes were restricted to self-reported operator job satisfaction, perceived operational and governance challenges, self-reported certification status, and recalled historical operator turnover (PDF Pages 4-13).
cross_tool_domains.reporting_bias: Moderate concern: no study protocol or pre-analysis plan is reported beyond university ethics approval (REB# 13NV048; PDF Page 4). Although reported themes match the stated interview/survey topics, quantitative presentation suffers from missing category labels on Figures 3 and 5 (PDF Pages 9, 13) and inconsistent subgroup totals for salary on PDF Page 7 (summing to 99 rather than 79), and qualitative coding procedures and direct verbatim quotes from Ontario interviews are minimally reported.
cross_tool_domains.selection_bias: High concern: Ontario qualitative interviews achieved participation from only 8 of 45 listed communities (8 of 28 confirmed to have a plant and operator) in relatively affluent, road-accessible southern Ontario 'best case' settings (PDF Pages 4-5, 17). The BC quantitative sample (n = 79) was a convenience sample recruited at an 'Operational Excellence Conference and Interactive Trade Show' without a known conference attendance denominator and under the unverified assumption that each respondent represented a distinct community (PDF Page 5), likely under-representing isolated or severely underfunded communities unable to send operators to a conference.

domain_ratings.justification: The study clearly states its empirical objective to investigate operator training, retention, and job satisfaction among First Nations water system operators in Ontario and British Columbia.

domain_ratings.domain_name: Screening S2: Do the collected data allow to address the research questions?
domain_ratings.justification: Semi-structured interviews in 8 Ontario communities and structured questionnaires from 79 BC operators directly captured data on certification, working conditions, compensation, job satisfaction, retention, funding, and band council support.

domain_ratings.domain_name: Qualitative 1.1: Is the qualitative approach appropriate to answer the research question?
domain_ratings.justification: Semi-structured qualitative interviews were appropriate for exploring sensitive institutional, political, and workplace challenges in First Nations communities where prior primary surveys were lacking.
domain_ratings.where_found: Methods — Semi-Structured Interviews in Ontario First Nations Communities (PDF Pages 4-5)

domain_ratings.domain_name: Qualitative 1.2: Are the qualitative data collection methods adequate to address the research question?
domain_ratings.justification: In-person and telephone semi-structured interviews covered relevant operational and governance themes, and refraining from audio recording in favour of paper questionnaires was a contextually justified adaptation to protect participants who feared repercussions.
domain_ratings.where_found: Methods — Semi-Structured Interviews in Ontario First Nations Communities (PDF Pages 4-5)

domain_ratings.domain_name: Qualitative 1.3: Are the findings adequately derived from the data?
domain_ratings.justification: The paper states only a single sentence that open-ended responses were coded and classified during analysis and key quotes retained, providing no description of the coding framework, analytic procedure, number of coders, or verification of handwritten interview notes.
domain_ratings.where_found: Methods — Semi-Structured Interviews in Ontario First Nations Communities (PDF Page 5)

domain_ratings.domain_name: Qualitative 1.4: Is the interpretation of results sufficiently substantiated by data?
domain_ratings.justification: While BC open-ended survey snippets are tabulated in Tables 2 and 3, the Ontario qualitative findings and governance interpretations rely on paraphrased bullet lists and narrative anecdotes without verbatim interview excerpts or participant-level attribution to substantiate claims.
domain_ratings.where_found: Results — Ontario First Nations (PDF Pages 6-7); Discussion (PDF Pages 14-16)

domain_ratings.domain_name: Qualitative 1.5: Is there coherence between qualitative data sources, collection, analysis and interpretation?
domain_ratings.justification: There is clear thematic continuity linking the semi-structured interview topics (certification, retention, job satisfaction, funding, Chief and Council relations) to the reported Ontario summaries and policy discussion.

domain_ratings.domain_name: Quantitative Descriptive 4.1: Is the sampling strategy relevant to address the research question?
domain_ratings.justification: Distributing questionnaires at the 7th Annual BC First Nation Water and Wastewater Operational Excellence Conference and Interactive Trade Show was a pragmatic, relevant way to access active First Nations water treatment operators from across British Columbia.
domain_ratings.where_found: Methods — Structured Interviews with Operators from British Columbia (B.C.) First Nations Communities (PDF Page 5)

domain_ratings.domain_name: Quantitative Descriptive 4.2: Is the sample representative of the target population?
domain_ratings.justification: Recruitment used convenience sampling at an 'Operational Excellence' conference rather than probability sampling across BC First Nations systems; authors merely assert representativeness while assuming without verification that each of the 79 operators came from a separate community, and conference attendance likely selects for better-resourced communities able to fund operator travel and shift coverage.
domain_ratings.where_found: Methods — Structured Interviews with Operators from British Columbia (B.C.) First Nations Communities (PDF Page 5)

domain_ratings.domain_name: Quantitative Descriptive 4.3: Are the measurements appropriate?
domain_ratings.justification: The newly constructed questionnaire lacked reported piloting or validation, relied solely on unverified self-report, allowed contradictory responses on job satisfaction (3 operators checked both satisfied and unsatisfied), exhibited an internal count error on salary (50 + 16 + 33 = 99 responses reported for N = 79), and lacked x-axis category labels in published Figures 3 and 5.
domain_ratings.where_found: Methods (PDF Page 5); Results — B.C. First Nations (PDF Pages 7, 9, 10, 13)

domain_ratings.domain_name: Quantitative Descriptive 4.4: Is the risk of nonresponse bias low?
domain_ratings.justification: The total number of operators attending the BC conference or invited to complete the questionnaire is never reported, making the survey response rate unknown, and item nonresponse was substantial on key items (e.g., salary non-disclosure reported as n = 33, 13 missing on vacation, 9 missing on experience, 8 missing on job satisfaction).
domain_ratings.where_found: Methods (PDF Page 5); Results — B.C. First Nations (PDF Pages 7, 10)

domain_ratings.domain_name: Quantitative Descriptive 4.5: Is the statistical analysis appropriate to answer the research question?
domain_ratings.justification: Descriptive frequency counts and percentages computed in Microsoft Excel were appropriate for an exploratory descriptive survey objective, notwithstanding minor graphical labelling omissions and the salary count discrepancy.

domain_ratings.domain_name: Mixed Methods 5.1: Is there an adequate rationale for using a mixed methods design to address the research question?
domain_ratings.justification: The authors provide a clear sequential exploratory rationale: given the small qualitative interview sample in Ontario (n = 8) and absence of prior surveys, qualitative findings were used to construct a structured survey for broader quantitative assessment and cross-provincial comparison in BC (n = 79).

domain_ratings.domain_name: Mixed Methods 5.2: Are the different components of the study effectively integrated to answer the research question?
domain_ratings.justification: Integration was achieved both at the methods/instrument level (building the BC survey items directly from themes identified in Ontario interviews) and at the interpretation level (jointly synthesizing Ontario and BC findings on certification, job satisfaction, O&M funding, and Chief and Council support).
domain_ratings.where_found: Methods (PDF Pages 5-6); Results (PDF Page 10); Discussion and Conclusions (PDF Pages 14-17)

domain_ratings.domain_name: Mixed Methods 5.3: Are the outputs of the integration of qualitative and quantitative components adequately interpreted?
domain_ratings.justification: The Discussion and Conclusions effectively combine qualitative institutional detail from Ontario (e.g., the 80:20 AANDC funding split, user fees, Band Council control over consumable purchases, local hiring dynamics) with quantitative prevalence patterns from BC to formulate policy recommendations.

domain_ratings.domain_name: Mixed Methods 5.4: Are divergences and inconsistencies between quantitative and qualitative results adequately addressed?
domain_ratings.justification: Substantial divergences between the Ontario qualitative sample (100% certified, all working full-time 35-40 hours/week with 3-5 weeks paid vacation) and the BC quantitative sample (42% uncertified/under-certified, half working 0-19 hours/week, 13 with no paid vacation) are not systematically reconciled, aside from a brief concluding remark that the 8 southern Ontario sites were expected to be 'best case' affluent/accessible systems.
domain_ratings.where_found: Results (PDF Pages 6-10); Discussion (PDF Page 10); Conclusions (PDF Page 17)

domain_ratings.domain_name: Mixed Methods 5.5: Do the different components of the study adhere to the quality criteria of each tradition of the methods involved?
domain_ratings.justification: Neither empirical component fully meets its methodological quality criteria: the quantitative descriptive survey suffers from convenience conference sampling without a known denominator, unpiloted measurement with contradictory dual-checked responses and a salary count error (50+16+33=99 for N=79), and missing figure axis labels, while the qualitative component lacks audio recording, coding transparency, and verbatim Ontario evidentiary support.

raw_response.overall_narrative_summary: Murphy et al. (2015) report an exploratory sequential mixed-methods study of First Nations drinking water operators in Canada, combining semi-structured qualitative interviews in 8 southern Ontario First Nations communities (March–August 2014) with a subsequent descriptive cross-sectional questionnaire completed by 79 First Nations water treatment operators at a provincial conference in British Columbia (October 2014). Appraised using the MMAT (2018) with the Quantitative Descriptive block (items 4.1–4.5), the study has a clear objective and coherent sequential design in which Ontario qualitative interviews directly informed the BC questionnaire and joint policy synthesis. However, per MMAT guidance that overall methodological quality cannot exceed the weakest component, the study carries high methodological concern. In the qualitative component, only 8 of 45 listed (28 confirmed) southern Ontario 'best case' communities participated, interviews were hand-recorded on paper rather than audio-recorded due to fear of repercussions, coding methods are described in a single generic sentence, and almost no verbatim quotes from Ontario interviews are presented. In the quantitative component, BC respondents were a convenience sample of attendees at an 'Operational Excellence' conference with no reported total attendance denominator (unknown response rate) and an unverified assumption that each operator represented a distinct community; measurements relied on an unvalidated self-report survey that allowed respondents to check both 'satisfied' and 'unsatisfied', exhibited an internal arithmetic error in salary frequencies (50 + 16 + 33 = 99 reported responses out of N = 79), and omitted x-axis category labels in published Figures 3 and 5. No objective water quality or administrative records were collected, and confounding by community remoteness, plant complexity, or revenue capacity was not controlled.
raw_response.overall_rating: High methodological concern (narrative MMAT judgment; no numeric score: sequential mixed-methods rationale and integration are clear, but overall quality is constrained by convenience conference sampling without a response-rate denominator, unvalidated self-report measurements with contradictory responses and a salary count error, high Ontario refusal rates, and minimal qualitative coding transparency)
raw_response.study_design_identified: Exploratory sequential mixed-methods study (semi-structured qualitative interviews in 8 southern Ontario First Nations communities informing a descriptive cross-sectional survey of 79 First Nations drinking water operators in British Columbia)
raw_response.where_found_summary: Study objective and regulatory background: Abstract (PDF Page 2) and Introduction (PDF Pages 3-4). Ontario qualitative sampling, data collection, and ethics (REB# 13NV048): Methods (PDF Pages 4-5). BC conference survey design and Excel descriptive analysis: Methods (PDF Pages 5-6). Ontario qualitative results: Results (PDF Pages 6-7). BC quantitative descriptive results, tables, and figures: Results (PDF Pages 7-13). Integrated institutional/governance analysis and policy recommendations: Discussion and Conclusions (PDF Pages 10, 14-17).
raw_response.why_tool_chosen: The study collects and integrates both primary qualitative data (semi-structured interviews with operators and community leaders in 8 Ontario First Nations communities, analyzed qualitatively) and primary quantitative data (a structured questionnaire administered to 79 BC First Nations operators, analyzed via descriptive statistics in Microsoft Excel) in an explicit sequential exploratory design where the qualitative phase defined the survey instrument and both strands were integrated in the Discussion and Conclusions. Per RISK_OF_BIAS.md §1, MMAT (Mixed Methods Appraisal Tool) with the Quantitative Descriptive component (4.1-4.5) is the exact matching instrument.
